slides.headline: The Space Between
slides.subheadline: Courtyards, thresholds and the quiet negotiations between shelter and exposure. An editorial reading of Japanese domestic space.
slides.kicker: THE TOKYO REVIEW · ARCHITECTURE & SPATIAL PHILOSOPHY

items.title: Make the boundary inhabitable
items.takeaway: The engawa accommodates sitting, passing and watching the garden. A common width is 1–1.3 m: an edge with enough depth to become a place.

items.title: Bring weather into the plan
items.takeaway: At Tadao Ando’s Azuma House, moving between interiors means crossing an open courtyard. Nature is not merely framed; it interrupts the domestic route.

items.title: Let gaps connect
items.takeaway: Moriyama House distributes domestic life across ten separate volumes. Garden paths become places for encounters rather than leftover space around a building.

slides.headline: A house interrupted by sky
slides.label: AZUMA HOUSE · OSAKA · 1976
slides.observation: The street-facing concrete façade has no windows; the open courtyard brings light and weather into the interior world. Privacy is gained at the perimeter, exposure accepted at the center.
notes: Read the courtyard as circulation, not scenery: crossing it is part of moving through the house.
Editorial reading: the compelling image is not empty concrete, but the resident’s passage between shelter and rain.

metrics.label: Site area · square meters
metrics.context: The Tokyo plot accommodates the owner’s dwelling and five rental apartments, with gardens and interconnected courtyards between volumes.

metrics.label: Detached volumes
metrics.context: The steel-sheet volumes do not touch. The house is an arrangement of buildings rather than a single enclosure.

metrics.label: Rental mini-houses
metrics.context: Each includes its own kitchenette and bathroom. Independent domestic facilities underpin the possibility of living alongside others.

slides.topic: The price of an open sky
slides.speaker: The Tokyo Review
slides.role: Editorial dialogue · not an architect quotation
slides.thesis: At Azuma House, the exposed crossing makes sunlight, wind and rain part of ordinary movement. Our reading: a route can cultivate attention as deliberately as a window frames a view.
slides.counterThesis: But an architectural lesson should not become a compulsory hardship. Our design position: preserve contact with weather while giving residents a sheltered alternative. Atmosphere should invite participation, not demand endurance.

slides.headline: Read the threshold on two axes

quadrants.title: Sheltered × Private
quadrants.body: Design brief: a screened edge for solitary sitting. Keep the garden visible without making the seated resident equally visible.

quadrants.title: Sheltered × Shared
quadrants.body: Design brief: a covered meeting edge. Allow conversation beside the circulation route, not across it.

quadrants.title: Exposed × Private
quadrants.body: Design brief: an inward courtyard. Distinguish the pleasure of stepping into rain from the obligation to cross it.

quadrants.title: Exposed × Shared
quadrants.body: Design brief: a garden passage with places to pause. Preserve a clear route home for the resident who does not want to socialize.

slides.headline: The common room was not prescribed
slides.subject: Ryue Nishizawa · Moriyama House, Tokyo · 2002–2005
slides.before: Design intent: none of the individual units was intended for communal use. Five self-contained mini-houses provided rental accommodation alongside the owner’s spaces.
slides.after: In occupation: the owner’s living room, Unit C, became an informal common room for lunches and drinks. The paths between buildings also became places to meet.
slides.takeaway: Our reading: architecture can make encounters possible without scripting every encounter. Leave room for residents to assign a space its social meaning.

impact.label: Rental mini-houses within the semi-communal arrangement—not a measured social-performance score.

slides.headline: White walls do not explain the house

myth.title: THE MYTH
myth.text: A restrained Japanese interior is principally a visual formula: pale surfaces, sparse furniture and nothing out of place.

reality.title: THE REALITY
reality.text: At Moriyama House, ten white volumes contain a life of films, music, books and informal gatherings. Windows avoid directly facing neighboring windows. The lesson is not compulsory emptiness; it is careful separation that permits both privacy and company.

slides.headline: Draw the life before the photograph

cards.title: Trace the rainy route
cards.desc: Mark every daily crossing between rooms. Identify where exposure is optional and where the plan makes it unavoidable.

cards.title: Draw the reciprocal view
cards.desc: For each window, draw both directions of sight. A view into the garden may also be a view into someone else’s room.

cards.title: Leave a place unassigned
cards.desc: Reserve somewhere to sit, meet or withdraw without fixing its use in advance. Judge the interval by what residents can make of it.

phases.label: MORNING — RELEASE
phases.detail: Bedding returns to storage; the sleeping area becomes available for daytime use. An adaptable room needs somewhere for its previous function to go.

phases.label: AFTERNOON — CONNECT
phases.detail: Sliding partitions open adjoining spaces for gathering. The boundary moves instead of requiring another permanently dedicated room.

phases.label: EVENING — ENCLOSE
phases.detail: Partitions close and bedding returns. The same floor supports another occupation: domestic capacity measured through time, not merely area.

slides.quote: Before removing another object, draw where someone will sit, what they will see, and where their belongings will go.

slides.headline: Draw the pause before the room.
slides.kicker: A spatial exercise: trace your arrival from the front door to your usual seat. Mark the place for shoes, the first sheltered view, and every obstruction.
slides.action: Save this exercise. Redraw your arrival.

slides.headline: An empty floor proves very little.

stat.label: Unoccupied floor — hypothetical study
stat.detail: Illustrative calculation, not measured research: 23.7 m² clear within a 25 m² room leaves 1.3 m² occupied. The percentage says nothing about comfortable seating, accessible routes, or adequate storage. Do not mistake vacancy for generosity.

steps.title: Draw the changeover
steps.body: Sketch sleeping, working, and hosting arrangements. For every object that moves, assign a storage location. Traditional room flexibility depends partly on putting bedding and furniture away.

steps.title: Separate light from view
steps.body: Shoji can obscure an exterior view while admitting light. Test a translucent sample at the intended opening before specifying the entire screen.

steps.title: Give the edge a purpose
steps.body: An engawa accommodates movement and sitting between room and garden. In your plan, test the seated view and the passing route together—not as separate drawings.

slides.headline: Borrow the function, not the costume.

do.title: RECOMMENDED
do.body: Specify what each element must accomplish: a screen filters daylight; a partition changes enclosure; an eave shelters the opening. These are working relationships, not decorative motifs.

dont.title: AVOID
dont.body: Do not add a timber platform and call the boundary resolved. An engawa also depends on shelter, exposure-appropriate finishes, and drainage away from the building.

items.title: Arrival tested
items.note: Rehearse entering with shoes, a wet umbrella, and a bag. Give each a destination without occupying the onward route.

items.title: Storage tested
items.note: Put away the actual bedding and movable furniture. Confirm that the proposed daytime arrangement can genuinely be achieved.

items.title: Light tested
items.note: Review the screen sample from the intended seat in morning and afternoon light, then check privacy with the interior illuminated.

items.title: Movement tested
items.note: Mock up partitions and furniture at full scale. Walk the route with doors open and closed; include the mobility aids occupants use.

components.label: EAVE — SHELTER
components.desc: The roof projects beyond the enclosure to shade openings and reduce rain exposure. Protection begins before the wall.

components.label: ENGAWA — OCCUPIABLE EDGE
components.desc: A timber or bamboo floor strip provides a place to pass, sit, and face the garden. Common widths are 1–1.3 m; large temples may have over 3 metres.

components.label: SHOJI — FILTER
components.desc: The sliding wood-and-paper screen softens daylight; closing it can obscure the view without extinguishing the changing light outside.​
